results.headline: Roman fort found in Wales could prove myth of emperor’s camp is real
results.evidence: Exclusive: Finds suggest account in medieval folklore of a camp near Frenni Fawr hill was rooted in reality Magnus Maximus, the Roman emperor who ruled Britain in the fourth century, led his troops against the Picts and Scots, but a theory that he also established a military camp near Frenni Fawr hill in Wales has so far been based on folklore. Now fourth-century coins, among other finds at a newly identified Roman fort in Pembrokeshire, suggest the medieval tale was rooted in reality, to the excitement of archaeologists. The fort was discovered by Dr Mark Merrony, a leading Roman specialist at the University of Oxford. He heads an excavation that is bringing to life a story about Magnus Maximus, as told in the Mabinogion, a collection of medieval epic tales of myth, magic and miracles. Merrony expressed excitement that this landscape held the only Roman military site close to where the Mabinogion places the emperor. “If Magnus Maximus was there, there must have been an army there,” he said. “It’s such a remote area but the tale mentions the easternmost peak of the Preseli Hills, which is where this site is. The presence of a heavily fortified Roman auxiliary fort may help unlock the mystery of a Mabinogion legend that has endured for nearly 1,700 years.” There had been no archaeological evidence for a Roman marching camp or fort on the summit of the Frenni Fawr or below it until now. Merrony discovered it about 2 miles (3.5km) south-west of the summit in 2024. Satellite imagery had shown a convincing outline in an overgrown field and, shortly after visiting it, his eye was caught by a Roman tile, which turned out to be the first of many. With financial support from Oxford University and crowdfunding, one of several planned excavations has just finished, confirming his theory of the site and its significance. Merrony said that before the dig, his brother, Nick, had jokingly asked him to find a couple of coins to prove the Magnus Maximus theory.

Their findings, published in Nature , suggest that key anatomical structures required for mammalian suckling, swallowing and breastfeeding behaviors evolved nearly 165 million years ago, long before the appearance of modern mammals. The findings describe a newly discovered species called Megacauda sungei, a large mammaliaform that lived during the Middle Jurassic Period in what is now Inner Mongolia, China. results.headline: A Distant Planet Emitted a Burst of Radio Waves. Why? - Nautilus
results.evidence: Astronomers pinpoint the origin of a 10 billion‑year‑old millisecond signal from space More than 10 billion years ago, something in a distant galaxy gave off an incredibly bright burst of radio waves which lasted just a few milliseconds. In new research published today in Science , our team tracked it back to its origin in a small galaxy filled with many young stars, when the universe was only one-fifth of its current age. Fast radio bursts like this one are a mystery scientists have been trying to unravel for almost 20 years since they were first discovered. Our discovery is the most distant such burst whose host galaxy has yet been identified. Finding a Radio Signal from 10 Billion Years Ago We detected the burst, dubbed FRB 20240304B, with the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa, using a system called MeerTRAP which is designed to catch fast-changing transient radio signals from space in real time. The different frequencies of the radio burst arrived at slightly different times. We call this effect “dispersion”, and it happens because the signal has travelled through a lot of electrically charged material in space on its journey to Earth. These calculations confirmed that we were looking at a galaxy 10.6 billion years ago. It contains only about 10 million times the mass of our Sun, which is a tiny fraction of the mass of our own Milky Way galaxy. The host galaxy appears to be a young galaxy still forming many stars, with a very low amount of metal content, and very different from many of the larger galaxies in which most other fast radio bursts have been found. Our discovery has shown for the first time that fast radio bursts were being produced all the way back to around 3 billion years after the Big Bang, during the period when the universe was most actively forming stars and galaxies. A landscape painted by rocks, wind, and water More than 10 billion years ago, something in a distant galaxy gave off an incredibly bright burst of radio waves which lasted just a few milliseconds. This lets us probe electrically charged matter across about 80% of cosmic history. Finding fast radio bursts at such large distances is difficult because of the combination of detecting increasingly faint bursts and identifying galaxies that are themselves extremely faint.

results.headline: Intensive breathwork reduces brain blood flow and alters neural communication
results.evidence: Intensive breathing exercises can reduce blood flow to the brain by up to 45% and alter communication between brain networks, according to a new brain-imaging study. Participants reported experiences resembling some effects of psychedelic drugs, including altered perception, vivid mental imagery, a sense of unity and changes in self-experience. The researchers, presenting the work at the ECNP Congress in Munich, say changes in brain communication, rather than reduced blood flow alone, appear to be key to the altered state. The study involved 30 healthy, experienced breathwork practitioners who performed high-ventilation breathwork during MRI scanning. Participants reported strong altered states of consciousness, describing a predominantly oceanic state – in other words, a deep feeling of connection to the universe - resembling that of a moderate to high dose of LSD or psilocybin, albeit with less pronounced visual effects. Brain imaging showed that global grey-matter cerebral blood flow fell by around 45% during the session, on average from 16.24 to 9.81 ml/100g/min. Those who reported stronger altered states also showed greater changes in the brain's default mode network, which is involved in self-reflection and self-related thinking. The researchers suggest that the intensity of the experience is not simply explained by reduced blood flow. Lead researcher Dr Christian Schmitz, Central Institute of Mental Health, Mannheim in Germany, said: " Many people who practice intensive breathwork report profound changes in perception and self-experience, yet the underlying brain mechanisms remain poorly understood. Our study suggests that these experiences are linked not only to marked changes in cerebral blood flow, but also to alterations in how key brain networks communicate". 'Co-Coordinator, Hana Adolphi said, " Breathwork is a legal, inexpensive and non-pharmacological intervention that may provide a valuable tool for studying altered states of consciousness. Understanding these mechanisms could also help inform future research into novel approaches for mental health treatment. Nevertheless, this was a relatively small study, and the findings should be considered preliminary. Larger studies will be needed to determine whether these brain changes have clinical relevance." Commenting, Dr Guy Fincham (Brighton and Sussex Medical School, UK) said: "This study is intriguing as it is starting to extend findings from recent breathwork research that intensive breathing practices may yield altered states of consciousness which individuals describe in ways analogous to psychedelic compounds, and under brain-imaging conditions. These findings are important because such altered subjective experiences may be harnessed for the improvement of mental health, and an accessible non-pharmacological route such a breathwork could prove invaluable for many. We should note that the study was uncontrolled and the sample was made up of experienced practitioners, so replication of this in breathwork-naïve participants using a randomised-controlled design will help determine whether these findings can translate more widely and produce therapeutic benefit".

evaluation.reason: A concrete, surprising neuroscientific finding that links a common practice to measurable physiological and neurological changes.
evaluation.strongest_fact: Intensive breathwork can reduce cerebral blood flow by up to 45% and alter communication within the brain's default mode network.

results.evidence: Using data from the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys, with help from artificial intelligence, an international team of scientists has discovered 70 new gravitational lenses—rare cosmic alignments that act as natural magnifying glasses.
